The Professional Pattern Room: Tools, Fabric Behaviour and Workroom

Advanced work starts with precise tools, a workroom that moves garments in a clear order, and a deep understanding of how fabric behaves before you cut it. This module sets up the professional standard you will use for every draft, toile and production order in the rest of the course.

At basic level, a tape measure, chalk and scissors are enough. At advanced level, you are no longer only sewing clothes. You are **making patterns that must be repeated exactly**, sometimes for twenty aso-ebi guests or a boutique order of thirty pieces. Every curve must be smooth, every notch must match its partner, and every piece must carry the information a cutter needs. That accuracy comes from the right tools used the right way.

The rule of thumb: **use the longest curve that fits the line**. A short French curve on a long princess seam makes a wobbly line made of many small curves joined together. A hip curve makes one smooth sweep. For an armhole, start with the French curve at the underarm where the curve is tightest, then blend into the straighter part near the shoulder.
Marking and transfer tools
**Tracing wheel**: copies lines from one paper to another, or from a pattern to fabric with carbon paper. A smooth-edged wheel is gentler on fine lace and silk; a serrated wheel grips paper better.
**Pattern notcher**: cuts a small slot in the edge of the paper so the notch is felt as well as seen. A neat 3 to 5 mm snip with scissors also works.
**Awl or bradawl**: punches a small hole inside the pattern to mark dart points, pocket positions and bust points. These are called drill holes.
**Pattern card or manila**: heavier than drafting paper. Final production patterns are traced onto card so edges do not tear after many uses.
**Pattern hooks and a rail**: keep all pieces of one style together, hung by a hole punched near the top of each piece.
Drill holes sit inside the stitching line
Punch a dart point drill hole about 1 cm inside the true point, not on it. If the hole sits exactly on the point, the chalk mark or snip on the fabric can show through after sewing.
What every finished pattern piece must say

A pattern that only you can understand is a draft. A pattern a cutter can use without asking questions is a **finished pattern**. Write clearly, in pencil first, then in marker once it is tested. Use the same layout on every piece so your eye always finds the information in the same place.
Labels on a finished pattern piece
Style name or number
Piece name and size
Cut quantity and fold
Grain line arrow
Notches and drill holes
Seam allowance stated
If any one of these is missing, the cutter has to guess, and guesses cost fabric.

The **grain line arrow** must run the full length of the piece, with arrow heads at both ends, so the cutter can measure from the selvedge at two points. The **cut quantity** is written as, for example, "Cut 2 self, cut 2 lining" or "Cut 1 on fold". Notches use a simple code: one notch on the front armhole, two notches on the back armhole. That way a front sleeve can never be sewn into a back armhole.

Amaka has the tools for precise curves, marking and storage, and a written list with real prices she found. She keeps her fabric scissors away from paper so they stay sharp.

Fabric behaviour: grain, bias, shrinkage and difficult fabrics
Identify lengthwise grain, crosswise grain and true bias on any fabric
Run and calculate a shrinkage test before cutting
Plan motif placement for lace and border prints
Adjust handling for sequinned, sheer and slippery fabrics

Two garments cut from the same pattern can hang completely differently if the fabric behaves differently. Advanced tailors read the fabric before they cut it. This lesson covers the four things that most often ruin good patterns: grain, bias stretch, shrinkage and fabrics that move or fray.
Grain and bias

Woven fabric has long threads running parallel to the selvedge (the finished edge). This is the **lengthwise grain**, also called straight grain. It is the strongest direction and stretches least. The threads going across, from selvedge to selvedge, are the **crosswise grain**, which has a little more give. The diagonal at 45 degrees to both is the **true bias**. Fabric cut on the bias stretches and drapes much more.
Straight grain versus true bias
Straight grain
True bias
Least stretch
Holds its shape
Used for most pattern pieces
Easy to cut and sew
Most stretch and drape
Clings to body curves
Used for bias binding, cowls
Hems can drop over time
Choose the grain on purpose: stability for structure, bias for drape.

To find true bias, fold the fabric so the crosswise edge lies along the selvedge. The fold line is the true bias. Bias strips for binding necklines and armholes are cut along this line. Bias-cut skirts and gowns should hang on a hanger for at least a day before you level the hem, because the bias drops unevenly as gravity pulls on it.
Shrinkage: test before you cut

Cotton, linen, many ankara prints and some locally woven fabrics shrink when first washed. If you cut a fitted gown to the exact size and the client washes it, it may become too tight. Always ask how the garment will be cleaned, then pre-treat the fabric the same way or test a sample.
Cut a square of 50 cm by 50 cm from the fabric, along the grain.
Mark the lengthwise direction with a thread or a pen arrow.
Wash and dry it the way the client will (hand wash and line dry, for example). Press it.
Measure both directions again.
Shrinkage percent = (before minus after) divided by before, times 100.
Worked example: shrinkage on a cotton print
For example, Bisi in Ibadan is making a fitted dress from a cotton print. She tests a 50 cm square before cutting.
After washing, the lengthwise side measures 48.5 cm and the crosswise side 49.5 cm.
Lengthwise shrinkage: (50 minus 48.5) divided by 50 times 100 = 3 percent.
Crosswise shrinkage: (50 minus 49.5) divided by 50 times 100 = 1 percent.
A 110 cm dress length would lose about 3.3 cm in length after the first wash if not pre-washed.
She decides to wash, dry and press the full fabric before cutting.
Because she tested, the dress keeps its length and fit after the client's first wash, and Bisi records "pre-wash, 3 percent length shrinkage" on the order card.
Lace, border prints and directional fabrics
**Corded and beaded lace**: lay out in a single layer, right side up, so you can see where motifs fall. Place the scalloped edge at the hem or sleeve end where possible, so you do not need to hem it.
**Border prints and aso-oke strips**: the pattern runs along one edge. Decide early whether the border goes at the hem, the sleeve or the neckline, and lay all pieces the same way.
**Directional prints and pile fabrics (velvet)**: use a "with nap" layout, meaning every piece points the same way up. This uses more fabric, so plan for it in your yardage.
**Matching**: for checks, stripes and large prints, match at centre front, side seams and where the sleeve meets the bodice at the front notch.
A pair of scissors
Single-layer cutting gives you control of every motif on lace and border prints.
Sequins, sheers and slippery fabrics

For **sequinned fabric**, remove sequins from the seam allowance before sewing, otherwise the needle breaks and the seam looks lumpy. Hand-stitch a few loose sequins back over bald areas after sewing. For **chiffon and organza**, cut between two layers of paper or on a fabric covered table so the fabric does not slide, use fine pins in the seam allowance only, and choose French seams so raw edges do not show through. For **satin and silky polyester**, use a fine sharp needle and test pressing temperature on a scrap, because these fabrics can melt or shine.

Before cutting any expensive fabric, check it on a light table or against a window for flaws: thin places, dye spots, pulled threads or misprints. Mark each flaw with a safety pin or a chalk circle on the wrong side, then lay your pieces so the flaws fall in the seam allowance or in waste. If a client brought the fabric, show her the flaw before you cut and note it on her order card, so nobody blames the cutting later.
Heat and synthetics

Many glittery and shiny fabrics are polyester or nylon and can melt under a hot iron. Always test on a scrap, use a press cloth, and keep the iron moving. Switch off and unplug the iron when you leave the table.

Setting up a production-ready workroom: machines, flow and electrical safety
Arrange a workroom so garments move in one direction from cutting to packing

When orders grow, the problem is rarely sewing skill. It is **flow**: fabric piled on the machine table, pattern pieces lost under offcuts, a client waiting while you look for her measurement card. A production-ready workroom arranges the work so each garment moves forward, never backwards.
One-way workroom flow

Cut and bundle
Sew
Press and finish
Inspect and pack
Arrange tables in this order so work moves forward and nothing doubles back.
Zones and bundles
**Receiving shelf**: every client's fabric is tagged with name, order number and due date the moment it arrives.
**Cutting table**: the largest clear surface. Nothing else lives here. Hip height is kindest to your back.
**Bundling**: after cutting, tie all pieces of one garment together with its order tag. Include the trims (zip, buttons, lining) in the bundle so the sewer never searches.
**Sewing zone**: machines with good light. Keep a small bin for threads and offcuts at each machine.
**Pressing zone**: iron, board, tailor's ham, sleeve board and press cloths, close to the sewing zone because you press after almost every seam.
**Finishing and packing**: hand sewing, buttons, final inspection, hanger and garment bag.
A person working at an organised workstation
An organised station saves minutes on every garment, and minutes add up to orders.

Machine

Limits

Industrial machines come with either a **clutch motor**, which runs all the time once switched on and can feel hard to control, or a **servo motor**, which only runs when you press the pedal, is quieter, and lets you set a slower speed. For a home workroom with unstable power, a servo motor is usually easier to control and uses less electricity because it is not running while you pin or press.
Worked example: planning a two-machine workroom
For example, Hauwa in Kaduna sews about six garments a week on one domestic machine and wants to double output for wedding season.
She times herself: finishing seams by zigzag takes about 25 minutes per gown.
She adds an overlocker, which finishes edges as it sews. Finishing drops to about 8 minutes per gown in her test.
On 12 gowns a week that saves about 17 minutes times 12, which is over 3 hours a week.
She keeps the domestic machine for buttonholes and decorative stitches and saves toward an industrial straight stitch for main seams.
She moves her pressing board next to the machines so she does not walk across the room after each seam.
Hauwa invests in the machine that removes her slowest step first, and rearranges the room so the work flows forward. The time figures are her own measurements, which is how you should decide too.
Electrical safety
Power rules for the workroom

Do not plug several machines and an iron into one extension board; irons draw a lot of current and overloaded boards can overheat. Use a voltage stabiliser or surge protector for machines. Run generators outside, never in a closed room, because exhaust contains carbon monoxide, which can kill without warning. Unplug the iron when not in use, keep cables out of walkways, and switch off a machine before changing the needle or clearing a jam.
Light and posture

Dark thread on dark fabric under a weak bulb causes crooked seams and tired eyes. Put a bright, white LED lamp at each machine and over the cutting table. Sit so your elbows are about level with the machine bed and your feet rest flat on the pedal. Every hour, stand, stretch your neck and shoulders, and look at something far away for a minute. A tailor with back pain cannot deliver on time.

Plan for power cuts too. Keep a rechargeable lamp at the cutting table so a blackout never catches you halfway through a cut, and do your heaviest pressing when you have steady supply. Some tailors batch all pressing for the day into one session on the generator or when grid power returns, which saves fuel. Keep fuel stored in a proper container, outside and away from the generator while it is hot.

Write your workroom rules on one sheet and stick it on the wall: where fabric is received, how bundles are tagged, power rules, and the end-of-day routine (unplug, clear tables, hang patterns). Anyone who helps you, an apprentice or a family member, follows the same sheet.

The parts of a garment the client never sees decide whether it still looks good after ten wears. Collars that curl, facings that roll out and gowns that cling to the body usually come from the wrong interfacing or lining, not from bad sewing. This lesson covers the hidden layers and how to tell the client how to care for the result.
Interfacing: the skeleton of collars and facings

Interfacing is an extra layer that adds firmness. **Fusible** interfacing has glue on one side and is ironed on. **Sew-in** interfacing is stitched in place and suits fabrics that cannot take heat or that would bubble with glue, such as some sequinned or very fine fabrics.

Behaviour
Good for
Woven fusible

Shirt collars and stands, cuffs, plackets, tailored jackets

Sew-in (organza, cotton lawn)

Match the weight: interfacing should be the same weight or lighter than the fashion fabric. Cut woven interfacing on the same grain as the piece it supports. For collars, many tailors interface only the **upper collar** or only the **under collar** depending on the look they want; test both on scraps to see which gives the roll you like.
Cut a test piece of fabric and interfacing, about 15 cm square.
Place glue side (the rough or shiny dots) down on the wrong side of the fabric.
Cover with a damp press cloth. Press down firmly without sliding, holding for about 10 to 15 seconds, then lift and move to the next spot.
Let it cool flat before moving it, because the glue sets as it cools.
Check: no bubbles, no glue on the right side, no shine or puckering. If it fails, change temperature or interfacing.
A tailored coat
The crisp collar and front of a tailored garment depend on the right interfacing underneath.
Linings for comfort and finish

A lining hides seams, stops lace from scratching, and helps a gown hang smoothly. In warm climates, breathable linings feel far better against the skin. Cotton lawn or cotton voile breathe well; polyester linings are cheaper and slide easily but can feel hot. For lace and sheer fabric, the lining colour changes the look completely: a nude or skin-tone lining makes lace look delicate, while a contrasting lining makes the pattern of the lace stand out. Show the client both options against the lace before cutting.
Care symbols: the five shapes

International care symbols are set out in the standard **ISO 3758**, maintained with input from GINETEX, the European textile care labelling association. There are five basic shapes. Dots inside the iron show temperature: one dot means low (about 110 degrees C), two dots medium (about 150 degrees C), three dots high (about 200 degrees C). A bar under a symbol means a gentler treatment and two bars mean very gentle. A cross through any symbol means do not.
The five care symbol shapes
Washtub: washing
Triangle: bleaching
Square: drying
Iron: ironing
Circle: professional cleaning
Every care label is built from these five shapes plus dots, bars and crosses.
Worked example: a care card for a lined lace gown
For example, Ifeoma in Enugu finishes a corded lace gown lined in polyester, with a concealed zip and some hand-sewn beads.
She tests a lace scrap: beads loosen in a machine wash, so she chooses hand wash cold, or professional dry cleaning.
Bleach would discolour the lace, so the triangle gets a cross.
Tumble drying could melt the polyester lining, so she writes "dry flat in shade".
Her pressing test worked at one dot on the wrong side with a cloth, so she adds the one-dot iron symbol and "press on the reverse".
She writes the card in plain words under each symbol, because many clients do not know the symbols.
The client receives a small printed card with symbols and words. If the gown is damaged by a hot iron later, Ifeoma has clear proof she gave correct instructions.
Words plus symbols
Always add plain words under each symbol, and send the same care note on WhatsApp with the delivery photo. The client then has it on her phone when the house help is ironing.

Keep a small stock of your best interfacing and linings, labelled by weight and colour, so you are not forced to buy whatever a market stall has on the day before a deadline. Record which combinations worked on each fabric in the test cards from the previous lesson.

In this module you take the extra measurements that pattern adjustments depend on, learn to read a figure respectfully, build your own size chart from real client data and check every number before it reaches paper.

A basic measurement card has bust, waist, hip, lengths and perhaps a shoulder. That is enough for loose styles. For fitted gowns, princess lines and set-in sleeves, those numbers hide important information. Two women with a 100 cm bust can need completely different patterns: one may have a broad back and small bust, the other a narrow back and a full bust. Shape measurements reveal the difference.

The **difference between full bust and high bust** is one of the most useful numbers in fitting. When it is large, the body is proportionally fuller at the bust than the frame. If you draft only from full bust, the shoulders and neckline become too wide and the armhole gapes. Experienced pattern makers often draft the frame from the high bust and then add bust room where it is needed, using a full bust adjustment, which you will practise in Module 5.
Back, shoulder and arm measurements
**Across back**: from armhole crease to armhole crease, about 10 to 12 cm below the nape, with arms relaxed. Too small a pattern here causes pulling across the back when she reaches forward.
**Across front**: crease to crease at the front, a few centimetres above the bust.
**Shoulder length**: from the side of the neck to the shoulder bone.
**Shoulder slope**: note whether shoulders are square, average or sloping. Some tailors measure from the nape around to the shoulder tip and down to the waist at front and back to capture it.
**Armhole depth and armscye**: around the arm at the armpit crease, plus the vertical distance from the shoulder to the underarm level.
**Upper arm (bicep)**: at the fullest part with the arm relaxed, then again with the elbow bent. Large upper arms need a sleeve adjustment.
**Nape to waist** and **front neck to waist** (centre front), to catch posture differences.
Measure the bra she will wear
Bust point height and span change with the bra. Ask the client to wear the bra she plans to wear with the garment, especially for wedding and owambe gowns.

Worked example: reading a client's numbers
For example, Ngozi in Port Harcourt measures a client for a fitted corset-style gown. High bust 92 cm, full bust 104 cm, across back 36 cm, bust span 20 cm, bust depth 27 cm.
Full bust minus high bust = 104 minus 92 = 12 cm. This is a large difference.
She notes that the frame (shoulders and back) is closer to a 92 cm body than a 104 cm body.
She plans to draft the bodice frame from the smaller measurement and add bust width with a bust adjustment.
Bust span of 20 cm means each bust point sits 10 cm from centre front; she marks this on the pattern.
Bust depth of 27 cm sets the bust point height, so darts and princess seams aim at the right place.
Instead of a gown with a gaping neckline and wide shoulders, Ngozi's first toile sits correctly on the frame and has room exactly where the bust needs it.

Take every shape measurement with the client standing in her normal posture, wearing thin fitted clothing, and with the tape snug but not pressing into the body. For lengths, tie a narrow tape or elastic around the natural waist first, so every vertical measurement ends at the same line. Mark the bust point lightly with a small sticker or a chalk dot on her clothing if she agrees, so the span and depth readings start from the same spot each time. If something is hard to measure alone, such as across back on a client with long braids, ask her to hold her hair up or ask an assistant to help.

Record measurements to the nearest half centimetre and always in the same order. A card with the order bust group, back group, arm group, length group means you can scan it quickly and spot a missing number before the client leaves.

Numbers tell you size. Your eyes tell you shape. Two clients with identical measurements can stand very differently: one leans back, one rounds her shoulders forward, one carries more on the seat, another more in front. These differences decide where wrinkles will appear on the finished garment. Advanced tailors observe them at the measuring stage and plan the pattern changes before cutting.
Look from three sides

Ask the client to stand naturally, feet slightly apart, arms relaxed, looking straight ahead. Do not ask her to stand up straight; you want her normal posture, because that is how she will wear the garment. Look from the front, the side and the back, and write short notes.

Simple checks that need no special tools

**Side seam check**: tie a narrow elastic or tape around the waist. From the side, look at whether it sits level. If it dips at the back, there may be a sway back; if it dips at the front, there may be a full abdomen pulling it down.
**Plumb line**: hang a weighted thread from the ear lobe at the side. Note where it falls relative to the shoulder, hip and ankle. This shows forward or backward lean.
**Shoulder level**: stand behind and place a ruler across both shoulder tips; see whether it tilts.
**Neck**: note a forward head or a thick neck base, which affect the back neckline and collars.
Photos with consent and privacy

Front, side and back photos help you check observations later and compare toile fittings. Only take them with clear permission, in fitted everyday clothing, never undressed. Explain why you want them and how you will store them. Keep them in a locked folder, not in your general gallery that syncs to shared devices, and never post them or send them to anyone else. Nigeria's Data Protection Act 2023 sets duties for anyone handling personal data, and body photos are among the most personal. Delete them when the order is complete unless the client agrees you keep them for future orders.

Not every observation needs a pattern change. Small differences, such as a few millimetres between shoulders, disappear in a loose kaftan and only matter in fitted styles. Decide which observations matter for the style she ordered, and focus your notes there. A fitted corset bodice is affected by almost everything on the checklist; a flowing boubou is affected mainly by shoulder slope and uneven shoulders, because the garment hangs from the shoulders.
Respectful language

Use neutral pattern words, not judgements. Say "your back has a lovely curve, so I will shorten the back waist to stop folds" rather than "you have a big bottom". Clients return to tailors who make them feel respected.
Worked example: planning changes before cutting

For example, Halima in Kano measures a client for a fitted lace bodice and a long pencil skirt. The numbers match a standard size, but her observation notes say: sway back, sloping shoulders, prominent seat.

For sloping shoulders, she plans to lower the shoulder point by about 1 cm and lower the underarm by the same amount to keep the armhole size.
For the prominent seat, she plans to deepen the back skirt darts slightly and add length at the centre back hem.
She writes each planned change and its amount on the order card, marked "to confirm at toile".
At the first fitting the toile already sits close to correct. The amounts are starting guesses, which the toile confirms or corrects, and she records the final amounts for the client's next order.

If you supply boutiques, sell ready-made iro and buba sets online, or make uniforms, you need sizes, not just individual measurements. Imported size charts were built on other populations and often do not match your clients, especially at the hip. The professional solution is to **build your own chart from your own measurement records**. You already have the data on your client cards.
A person working with a table of data
Your client cards are a dataset; a size chart is that data organised.
Step 1: gather and clean the data
Copy bust, waist, hip, across back and key lengths from your client cards into a notebook table or a spreadsheet such as Google Sheets. Use first names or numbers only, not full names.
Remove obvious errors, such as a waist larger than the hip by 30 cm on a client you remember as pear-shaped. Re-check with the client if possible.
Sort the rows by bust (for tops) or by hip (for skirts and trousers).
Look at the range: smallest and largest values, and where most clients cluster.
Step 2: choose your base size and intervals

The **base size** is the size you draft and fit first, ideally the size your clients wear most often, because errors in fitting are smallest near the middle. The **interval** is the jump between sizes. Many charts use a jump of about 4 to 5 cm in bust, waist and hip between neighbouring sizes; larger sizes often use bigger jumps. There is no single correct number: use what your data shows. If your clients' hips are proportionally larger than their bust compared with an imported chart, your chart should show that.

Step 3: body chart and garment chart

A **body measurement chart** tells the buyer which size to choose: "if your bust is 96 to 100 cm, choose size 14". A **finished garment chart** tells you and the buyer the actual size of the item: "the size 14 buba measures 116 cm around the bust". The difference between them is the **ease**, and it changes by style. A fitted gown may have only a few centimetres of ease at the bust, while a buba has a lot. Always publish both when you sell online, because buyers then compare with a garment they already own.
Worked example: a four-size chart for ready-made buba sets
For example, Tola in Lagos has 60 past client cards and wants to sell ready-made iro and buba on Instagram and WhatsApp.
She sorts by bust. Most clients fall between 92 and 112 cm, with the biggest cluster around 100 to 104 cm.
She sets her base size as the size for a 100 to 104 cm bust and calls it M.
She uses an interval of 5 cm and gets S (95 to 99), M (100 to 104), L (105 to 109), XL (110 to 114).
She checks hips in each bust group and sees they are on average larger than an imported chart suggests, so she sets her hip ranges from her own data.
She decides the buba should have 16 cm of ease at the bust and writes the finished bust: S 115, M 120, L 125, XL 130 cm (taking the top of each range plus ease).
She posts both charts together with a measuring guide.
Tola's chart reflects her real buyers, so returns and exchange requests are fewer. The ranges and ease figures are her own choices from her data, which is exactly how a chart should be made.

Lengths need sizes too. Check nape to waist, shoulder to floor and sleeve length in each size group. In many datasets height varies independently of width, so a tall size 10 and a short size 10 may both exist among your clients. You can handle this with a standard length plus a note that you will shorten or lengthen on request, or with separate regular and tall lengths if your data shows enough tall buyers to justify it.
Name sizes clearly
Clients may say "size 14" from UK labels or "L" from other brands, and these do not agree between brands. Publish centimetre ranges beside every size name so nobody guesses.

Review your chart every six months. Add new client data, and track exchanges: if many people who ordered L say it is tight at the hip, the hip range for L is wrong. A size chart is a living document, not a one-time task.

Every advanced tailor has a story about a gown cut from one wrong number. A tired evening, a tape that slipped, a 7 written like a 1. The fix is not to measure more carefully once; it is to build **checks** into your routine that catch errors automatically, just as an accountant checks that totals add up.
Cross-checks that should add up
**Across front plus across back** should be noticeably less than the full bust, because neither includes the sides under the arms.
**Waist** is normally smaller than **hip**. If the waist is larger, re-check and confirm with your eyes: some bodies really are like that, but confirm.
**Nape to waist** and **front neck to waist** differ by a few centimetres on most bodies; a very large difference suggests posture or a measuring error.
**Left and right**: measure shoulder length and arm length on both sides once. Differences over about 1 cm are worth noting.
**Repeat the key three**: bust, waist and hip taken twice. If the two readings differ by more than about 1 cm, take a third.
A person verifying data on a screen
Checking numbers against each other catches the errors that careful measuring alone misses.

Cross-check totals

Run this loop before any number goes onto drafting paper.
Measuring a garment she loves

Ask the client to bring a garment that fits her well, in the same type of style. Lay it flat, button or zip it closed, and measure across the bust, waist and hip, doubling the flat measurement. Measure shoulder width, sleeve length, armhole and length. Compare with her body measurements. The difference is the ease she likes. This is powerful information, because ease preference is personal: some clients like a close fit, others like room to move and breathe in the heat.
Worked example: catching an error with a garment check
For example, Chioma in Abuja measures a client's bust at 98 cm and hip at 104 cm. The client brings a well-fitting fitted dress.
Flat dress bust is 51 cm, so the circumference is 102 cm: ease of 4 cm over a 98 cm bust. Reasonable.
Flat dress hip is 50 cm, so 100 cm around. That is smaller than her measured 104 cm hip, which is impossible for a woven dress without stretch.
Chioma checks the fabric: it is a woven without stretch, so one number is wrong.
She re-measures the hip with the client standing with feet together and gets 98 cm. The first reading had the tape dipping at the back.
She corrects the card, notes the date, and adds 2 cm ease, matching the dress the client likes.
The garment check exposed a 6 cm error that would have produced a loose, baggy skirt. The client never knew there was a problem.
Tolerances and version-controlled records

A **tolerance** is the amount of difference you accept. For example, you might decide that a repeat bust reading within 1 cm is acceptable, but anything more is retaken. Write your tolerances on your card template so apprentices follow the same rule.

Some tailors also measure the client on two occasions before an important garment such as a wedding gown, a few weeks apart, because weight can change before big events. If the numbers move, use the latest set for the final fitting and keep the toile seams generous until the last fitting. Plan this into the timeline you agree with the client, so the extra measuring session is expected, not a surprise.

Bodies change with time, pregnancy, illness and age. Never overwrite old measurements. Add a new dated column each time you measure, so the card shows history. For repeat clients, re-measure the key three at every new order, even if she says nothing has changed. If you keep cards digitally, back them up and protect them with a password, and store only what you need: name, phone, measurements, notes on fit. Delete records of clients who ask you to.

Write numbers clearly and include units. Cross your sevens and write a full zero before the decimal point, for example 0.5 cm, not .5 cm. Small habits like these stop an apprentice from reading 1 for 7 or missing a decimal point when the card is copied into the pattern.
Fitting notes are gold
Add the final pattern changes from each fitting to the card, for example "sway back 1.5 cm, lower right shoulder 0.8 cm". Next time, these go straight onto the pattern before the first toile.

Advanced Drafting: Flat-Pattern Manipulation, Princess Lines, Sleeves and Collars

With a fitted block in hand, you can create almost any style on paper. This module teaches slash-and-spread and pivot methods for adding fullness, yokes and flare; drafting and truing princess-line panels; drafting set-in, puff and bishop sleeves that fit the armhole; and drafting stand, Peter Pan and shirt collars that sit neatly at the neck.
Flat-pattern manipulation: yokes, gathers, pleats and flare
Explain the difference between slash-and-spread and pivot methods
Separate a yoke from a block and transfer the dart into it
Add controlled fullness for gathers or pleats
Turn a straight skirt block into a flared skirt by closing darts

**Flat-pattern manipulation** means changing a tested block on paper to create a new style, without drafting from zero. Because the block already fits, every style made from it keeps the same fit at the important points: neck, shoulder, bust and waist. Two techniques do almost all the work.
Two ways to change a pattern
Slash and spread
Pivot
Cut lines on a copy of the block
Open the cuts to add width
Very visual, good for learning
Uses more paper and tape
Trace the block, then rotate it
Rotate around a fixed point
Fast and clean once practised
No cutting of the master copy
Both give the same result; choose the one that suits the change and your experience.
Always work on a **copy** of the block, never the master. Mark the grain line, bust point and notches on the copy before you start, so you can see how they move.
Separating a yoke

A yoke is a fitted section across the shoulders, chest or hips, joined to a looser lower part. On a bodice, a front yoke line can be drawn from the armhole to the centre front, passing near the tip of the shoulder dart. Cut along the yoke line. Then close the part of the dart that falls inside the yoke, and true the yoke seam. The yoke now fits the shoulders without a dart, because the dart has been absorbed into the seam.
Adding fullness for gathers and pleats
On the lower piece below the yoke, draw vertical slash lines about 3 to 5 cm apart, from the yoke edge to the hem.
Cut along each line from the top to the hem, leaving a tiny paper hinge at one end if you want fullness only at the top.
Spread each cut evenly on fresh paper. The total spread is the extra width you want gathered or pleated.
Tape down, redraw the yoke edge and hem as smooth curves, and mark the gathering zone between two notches.
For pleats, fold the paper along the pleat lines before cutting the top edge, so the edge is correct when the pleats are closed.

How much fullness? A common starting point for soft gathers is about one and a half times the finished length of the seam; for heavy gathers about two times. A fabric like chiffon gathers beautifully at two times, while a stiff aso-oke would look bulky. Test on a strip of your fabric before deciding.
A designer drafting ideas on paper
Flat-pattern manipulation turns one tested block into many styles on paper.
From straight skirt to flared skirt

Take the front skirt block with its waist dart. Draw a line from the dart point straight down to the hem, parallel to the grain. Cut up this line to the dart point. Close the dart at the waist; the slash opens at the hem. The dart width has become **flare at the hem**, and the waist still fits. For more flare, add further slash lines and spread them at the hem. A circle skirt is the extreme version of the same idea.
Worked example: a yoked peplum blouse with gathers
For example, Zainab in Abuja wants to make a yoked blouse with a gathered peplum from her tested bodice block for an ankara set. The front waist measures 20 cm on the quarter pattern.
She draws a front yoke line 8 cm below the shoulder at the armhole, curving to 12 cm below the neck at centre front, and closes the shoulder dart into it.
She shortens the bodice to the natural waist and transfers the waist dart into a seam joining the peplum.
For the peplum, she wants 1.5 times fullness. The front waist seam is 20 cm on the quarter, so the peplum top edge needs 30 cm.
She draws a 20 cm by 15 cm rectangle, slashes it into five strips and spreads each gap by 2.5 cm at the top, giving 30 cm.
She marks notches at the side and centre front and tests the peplum in calico before cutting the ankara.

The blouse fits at the shoulders and waist because both come from the block, and the peplum has even, controlled fullness. Zainab saves the yoke and peplum pieces as a new style in her pattern register.

The pivot method gives the same results without cutting. To move a dart, trace the block from the centre front up to the first dart leg. Hold the paper down with an awl on the bust point, rotate the block until the dart leg closes onto the traced line, and trace the rest. The opening appears wherever you started tracing. Once you are confident, pivoting is faster and keeps your block copies intact, which matters when you work with expensive pattern card. Whichever method you use, label the new piece with its own style name and date, because a manipulated pattern is a new pattern.
True every new seam

After any manipulation, place the two seams that will be sewn together side by side and check they are the same length and meet at a smooth angle. This is called truing. Fix it on paper, never on fabric.

A princess seam is a long curved seam that runs over the bust and down towards the hem. Unlike a dart, which is a fold that stops at a point, a princess seam is a full seam that divides the bodice into panels. It can start at the shoulder or at the armhole. Because the shaping is spread along the whole seam, princess lines can fit curvy bodies very closely, which is why they are common in fitted owambe gowns, corset dresses and mermaid styles.

Armhole princess

Drafting an armhole princess
Trace the front block with shoulder (or side) dart and waist dart, bust point marked.
Pivot or slash so the dart moves to the armhole: draw a curved line from about one third of the way up the front armhole to the bust point, cut it, close the original dart.
Join the armhole dart to the waist dart through the bust point with a smooth curve. This is the princess line.
Separate the centre front panel and the side front panel along the line, each keeping its own side of the dart.
Add notches: one about 6 to 8 cm above the bust point and one about 6 to 8 cm below, plus one at the waist.
True the seam: the two sides of a princess seam are different shapes but must be the same length between notches, or have a deliberate small ease over the bust.
Ease over the bust

On the side front panel, the curve over the bust is longer than the matching centre front edge. Some pattern makers keep a small amount of ease there (often a few millimetres) to shape over the bust; others make them exactly equal. Decide, then mark it between the bust notches so sewers ease it in evenly.
A dress

Shaping complex figures with panels

Each princess seam is a place where you can add or remove width independently. On a full bust, you can add width to the side front panel at bust level and blend it back to nothing at the waist and armhole. On a client with a small waist and full hips, you can take in each seam at the waist and let it out at the hip. A gown with front and back princess seams plus side seams has **six to eight seams** where you can adjust, so the fit can follow almost any curve.

The rule is to **share the change**. If the gown needs to lose 4 cm at the waist, take a little from each seam rather than all from the side seams. Large changes in one seam distort the shape and pull the grain off.
Worked example: sharing a waist reduction across panels
For example, Efe in Benin City makes a mermaid gown in lace over a satin lining. At the toile fitting, the waist is 6 cm too big all round, while bust and hip are correct.
The gown has front and back princess seams on both sides plus two side seams: six seams in total.
Each seam has two edges, giving twelve edges. 6 cm divided by 12 = 0.5 cm taken from each edge at the waist.
She marks 0.5 cm in at the waist notch on each panel edge and blends back to the original line about 10 cm above and below.
She re-trues each seam pair so lengths still match.
On the satin lining, she makes the same change so the lining and lace move together.
The waist is reduced evenly, the grain stays straight down each panel, and the lace motifs remain balanced. One large change at the side seams would have pulled the princess lines towards the sides.

Princess panels also make lace placement easier. Because each panel is cut separately, you can centre a large lace motif on the centre front panel and mirror motifs on the side panels, something impossible on a single-piece bodice. Lay each panel on the lace in a single layer, right side up, and turn the second side front panel over so the motifs mirror. Cut lining panels from the same pattern pieces so the lining follows exactly the same shaping.
Extending to the hem

For a fitted gown, extend the princess lines from the waist through the hip to the hem. For a mermaid or trumpet shape, decide the flare point, often around knee level, and add flare to each panel edge from that point to the hem. Add the same amount to both edges of each seam so panels stay balanced, and true the hem as one smooth curve when all panels are placed side by side.

Measure the front and back armhole on the bodice pattern
Draft a one-piece set-in sleeve with a cap that fits the armhole

Turn the basic sleeve into puff and bishop sleeves

A beautifully fitted bodice is ruined by a sleeve that twists, pulls or will not go into the armhole. The secret is that **the sleeve is drafted from the armhole**, not only from the arm. The curve at the top of the sleeve, called the **sleeve cap** or sleeve head, must match the length of the armhole with a small, planned amount of extra length called cap ease.
Measurements you need
**Front armhole and back armhole lengths**, measured on the bodice pattern along the stitching line, with a tape on its edge or a flexible curve. Measure from shoulder point to side seam for each.
**Upper arm (bicep)** plus ease. For a fitted woven sleeve, a few centimetres of ease is usual; for a loose sleeve, much more.
**Sleeve length** from shoulder point to wrist, with the arm slightly bent.
**Wrist** or the desired sleeve opening for short or three-quarter sleeves.
Cap height decides fit and movement

The **cap height** is the distance from the top of the sleeve down to the bicep line. A **high cap** makes a narrow sleeve that hangs smoothly with the arm down, which looks elegant in a fitted gown but restricts lifting the arm. A **low cap** makes a wider sleeve with more movement, as in shirts, kaftans and workwear. Both sleeves can fit the same armhole: as the cap gets lower, the sleeve gets wider.

Drafting a basic set-in sleeve
Draw a vertical centre line equal to the sleeve length. The top point is the crown.
Choose a cap height and square a bicep line across at that depth.

From the crown, draw a straight line down to the bicep line on the back side, equal to the back armhole length. Repeat on the front side with the front armhole length. Where they meet the bicep line sets the sleeve width.
Check the bicep width against her upper arm plus ease. If it is too narrow, lower the cap height slightly and redraw; if too wide, raise it.
Divide each diagonal into parts and draw the cap curve: outward above the line near the crown, inward below it near the underarm, with the front scooped a little more than the back.
Draw the underarm seams down to the wrist width, mark one notch at the front and two at the back, and mark the crown notch to match the shoulder seam.

Measure the finished cap curve. It should be longer than the armhole by the cap ease you want. For a fitted blouse in medium-weight woven fabric, many pattern makers aim for roughly 2 to 4 cm; shirts and knit tops need little or none; heavy fabrics take less because they do not ease well. If the curve is too long, flatten the cap slightly; if too short, add a little height or curve.
Worked example: checking cap ease
For example, Adaeze in Owerri drafts a sleeve for a fitted crepe dress. On her bodice, the front armhole measures 22 cm and the back 23.5 cm. Her client's bicep is 32 cm.
Total armhole = 22 + 23.5 = 45.5 cm.
She wants about 3 cm of cap ease for crepe, so the cap curve should be about 48.5 cm.
With her first cap height, the bicep width comes out at 31 cm, less than the 32 cm arm. She lowers the cap height by 1 cm and redraws; the bicep is now about 34 cm, giving 2 cm ease.
She measures the new cap curve: 49.5 cm, which is 4 cm over the armhole. She flattens the curve slightly near the crown and remeasures: 48.6 cm.
She sews a calico test sleeve into the toile and checks it hangs without twisting.
The sleeve eases smoothly into the armhole with no puckers, and the client can lift her arm comfortably. Adaeze writes the cap height and ease on the sleeve pattern for future use.

A well-drafted sleeve cap is the difference between a homemade and a professional blouse.
Puff and bishop sleeves

**Puff sleeve**: slash the cap from crown to bicep in several lines and spread at the top only. Raise the crown by a few centimetres so the fullness stands up. Gather the extra into the armhole between the notches.
**Bishop sleeve**: slash from wrist up to the cap and spread at the bottom, adding length at the back of the wrist so it blouses over a cuff. Gather into a cuff or elastic.
**Both**: keep the armhole notches and underarm curve unchanged so the sleeve still fits the bodice.
Sew the sleeve test first
Sleeves are cheap to test and expensive to get wrong in lace. Always sew one sleeve in calico into the toile armhole before cutting the real fabric.

Collars sit at the most visible part of a garment, right next to the face. A collar that stands away from the neck, twists at the front or shows its seam ruins the whole look. Every collar is drafted from one key number: the **neckline length** of the pattern, measured on the stitching line from centre back to centre front. Measure the back neck and front neck separately, because collar notches must line up with the shoulder seam.

Measure back and front neck

Never draft a collar before the neckline has been fitted, or the collar will not match.
Mandarin or stand collar

The stand collar is a narrow band that stands up around the neck. It is used on kaftans, senator-style tops and many blouses. Start with a rectangle: length equals half the neckline (centre back to centre front), height equals the stand height you want, often 3 to 4 cm. A straight rectangle stands away from the neck. To make it hug the neck, **raise the front end** of the lower edge by about 1 to 1.5 cm and draw a smooth curve from the centre back to the raised point, then curve the top edge parallel. The more you curve it upward, the closer it sits to the neck.
A robe with a neat neckline
Stand collars and neat neck finishes are common on kaftans and robe-style garments.
Peter Pan collar

A Peter Pan collar lies flat on the shoulders with rounded ends. It is drafted directly from the bodice. Place the front and back bodice patterns together at the neck point of the shoulder seam. Overlap the shoulders at the armhole end by about 1 to 2 cm. This overlap shortens the outer edge slightly, which gives the collar a small roll so the seam hides under it. Trace the neckline, then draw the outer edge parallel at the collar width you want, often 6 to 8 cm, rounding the front.
**No overlap**: collar lies completely flat, and the neck seam may show.
**1 to 2 cm overlap**: slight roll, seam hidden, the usual choice.
**Large overlap**: more roll and stand, moving towards a different collar style.
Shirt collar with separate stand
Draft the stand like a curved mandarin collar, adding the button extension at the front end (equal to the button stand width on the shirt front).
Draw the collar on top of the stand: its lower edge follows the top edge of the stand but curves **downward** at the front, the opposite direction to the stand.
Make the collar slightly deeper than the stand at the back, often 1 to 1.5 cm more, so it covers the stand seam when it folds over.
Draw the collar point shape at the front, with the point length and spread to suit the style.
Add notches at centre back and at the shoulder position on both stand and collar.
Cut the under collar slightly smaller than the upper collar at the outer edge, a few millimetres, so the seam rolls to the underside.
Worked example: a stand collar for a kaftan
For example, Aisha, a tailor in Sokoto, is drafting a stand collar for a man's kaftan. On the pattern, the back neck is 8.5 cm and the front neck 12 cm, centre back to centre front.
Half neckline = 8.5 + 12 = 20.5 cm. She draws a rectangle 20.5 cm long and 3.5 cm high, plus a 1.5 cm button overlap at the front.
She marks a shoulder notch 8.5 cm from centre back.
She raises the front end of the lower edge by 1.2 cm and draws a smooth curve from centre back, then curves the top edge parallel.
She cuts the collar on grain, interfaces one layer with woven fusible, and tests it on the calico toile.
The collar sits close at the back but slightly away at the front, so she raises the front another 0.5 cm and retests.
The final collar sits evenly around the neck with the shoulder notch matching the shoulder seam. Aisha writes the curve amount on the pattern so every kaftan in that size gets the same collar.
Stretching necklines

Curved necklines are partly on the bias and stretch easily while you handle them. Staystitch the bodice neckline just inside the seam line immediately after cutting, so it keeps the length your collar was drafted to fit.
Keep a set of collar patterns for each neckline in your block range. Once a collar works on a tested neckline, it works on every style made from that block.

This module applies your drafting skills to garments your clients wear every week: the Yoruba iro and buba, and the West African kaftan and boubou. You then learn to turn a single tested pattern into a production pattern set with markers that save fabric, and to grade it across a full size range using grade rules.

Iro and buba is a Yoruba women's outfit. The **buba** is a loose blouse, the **iro** is a wrapper tied around the waist, and the outfit is commonly completed with a **gele** (head tie) and sometimes an **ipele** or **iborun** worn over the shoulder. Fabrics range from ankara to lace and the hand-woven **aso-oke**. Because the buba is loose, many tailors think it needs no skill. At advanced level, a buba that hangs evenly, does not pull at the underarm and has a crisp neckline is a mark of quality.
A loose woman's blouse
The buba is loose, but a professional one still hangs evenly and moves freely.
The kimono-cut buba

Many bubas are **kimono-cut**: the sleeve is cut in one piece with the body, with no armhole seam. This saves time and suits wide, flowing sleeves. The pattern is a T-shape folded at the shoulder line.
Measure bust, hip, shoulder to desired length (often hip length or longer), and the sleeve length from the neck point over the shoulder to the desired sleeve end.
Decide the ease. A relaxed buba often has 20 cm or more of ease at the bust; a more fitted modern buba less. Write your choice.
Draw a centre line for the length. Square across at the shoulder line. Mark the half width at bust level: (bust plus ease) divided by 4 for each quarter.
From the neck point, draw the sleeve along the shoulder line, sloping down slightly (a few centimetres over the sleeve length) so the sleeve does not stand up stiffly.
Draw the underarm curve from the sleeve end down to the side seam. A deep curve gives a batwing look; a shallow, higher curve gives a closer sleeve.
Draw the neckline: front deeper than back. Add a facing pattern 5 to 6 cm wide that follows the neckline.

Underarm gussets

When a kimono sleeve is made closer to the body, lifting the arm pulls the whole garment up and can tear the underarm seam. A **gusset** solves this: a small diamond or triangle of fabric set into a slash at the underarm. It adds length exactly where the arm needs to move. Cut gussets on the bias for extra give, and reinforce the slash point with a small piece of fusible interfacing before cutting into it.
Aso-oke and sleeves

Aso-oke is woven in narrow strips joined together and can be stiff. Plan where the strip joins fall before cutting, so they run straight and symmetrically, and avoid deep, curved underarms that the stiff fabric resists.
From wrapper to tailored iro

The traditional iro is a rectangle of fabric wrapped and tucked at the waist. Many clients now ask for a **ready-to-wear iro** that stays in place. Common methods include adding a waistband with hooks or ties, sewing in an elasticated back section, or shaping it as a wrap skirt with a fixed inner panel. Measure the waist and hip, and decide the overlap at the front (enough that it does not open when walking). Keep the outer layer long and draped so it still looks like a wrapper.

Finish the buba neckline with care, because it frames the face and the gele. Staystitch the neckline after cutting, interface the facing lightly, understitch the facing to the seam allowance so it rolls inside, and press over a tailor's ham. For lace bubas, a narrow bias binding in a matching lining fabric often looks cleaner than a wide facing that shows through the lace.
Worked example: drafting a set of buba and tailored iro

For example, Yetunde in Abeokuta drafts a buba and tailored iro for a client with bust 104 cm, hip 112 cm, waist 90 cm. The client wants a kimono sleeve to the elbow and wants the iro to stay in place for dancing.
She chooses 20 cm bust ease: (104 + 20) divided by 4 = 31 cm for each quarter at bust level.
Hip check: she needs at least (112 + 8) divided by 4 = 30 cm at hip level for comfort. Her 31 cm side line is enough, so the side seam can run straight.
Because the client wants a closer sleeve, she adds a bias-cut gusset of 10 cm by 10 cm at each underarm.
For the iro, she adds a 4 cm waistband sized to 90 cm plus 2 cm ease, with a 25 cm front overlap and two hooks and bars.
She tests the buba in calico and asks the client to lift both arms and dance a few steps.
The buba hangs evenly and does not lift when the client raises her arms, and the iro stays secure while looking like a traditional wrapper. Yetunde saves both as a style in her pattern register.

The **boubou** is a flowing, wide-sleeved robe worn across West Africa. It is known by many names, including **babban riga** in Hausa, **mboubou** in Wolof and **grand boubou** in French-speaking countries. The grand boubou is the formal version, often richly embroidered and worn over a caftan and loose trousers. Boubous are often made from cotton damask called **bazin**, or other cotton fabrics. A **kaftan** in Nigerian usage is usually a long tunic, narrower than a boubou, often with a stand collar or embroidered neckline, worn by men and women.
A long flowing robe
Wide robes are drafted mostly from rectangles, so fabric width and neckline work matter most.
The rectangle principle

A traditional boubou is built from large rectangles. The main piece is folded at the shoulder line, so the front and back are one piece with a neck opening cut in the middle. The width usually spans from wrist to wrist with the arms held out, which forms the sleeves. Side seams are sewn from the hem up to the underarm, leaving the sleeve openings free. Because the shape is simple, the quality is in the proportions, the neckline and the finishing.
Measure arm span from wrist to wrist with arms held out, and shoulder to ankle (or desired length).
Main piece: width = arm span (or the sleeve width the style needs); length = 2 times the garment length, folded at the shoulder.
Mark the centre point of the fold. This is the centre of the neckline.
Mark side seams: from the hem up to the underarm point, leaving the sleeve opening (for example 30 to 40 cm from the fold).
Draw the neckline: a round or boat neck, with a front slit if needed for the head to pass through. Draft a facing that follows it.

Check fabric width before drawing anything, because it decides the construction.
When the fabric is too narrow

Many fabrics are narrower than an adult's arm span. For example, ankara is often about 115 to 120 cm wide (check yours), while an arm span may be 160 cm or more. The solution is to **add side panels**: the centre panel uses the full fabric width, and two side panels are joined to make up the total. Place the seams symmetrically, and match the print where they join. In some traditional garments, extra triangular pieces (gores) are set into the sides to add swing at the hem.
Worked example: planning fabric for a woman's boubou
For example, Hadiza in Kano is making a woman's boubou. Arm span 158 cm, shoulder to ankle 138 cm. The fabric is 116 cm wide.
Main piece needs to be 158 cm wide, but the fabric is only 116 cm. Shortfall = 158 minus 116 = 42 cm.
She adds two side panels, each 21 cm finished plus 1.5 cm seam allowance on each side: 24 cm wide each.
Centre panel length = 2 times 138 = 276 cm, plus 3 cm hem allowance on each end: 282 cm.
Each side panel also runs the full folded length, 282 cm. Two side panels of 24 cm fit side by side in one 116 cm width, so they need one more 282 cm length.
Total fabric: 282 + 282 = 564 cm, about 5.64 m, plus allowance for the neckline facing and print matching. 6 yards is only about 5.49 m, which is not enough, so she buys 7 yards (about 6.4 m).
Hadiza calculates before she buys, finds that a standard 6 yards would be short, and buys 7. One yard is 0.9144 m, so always convert carefully when fabric is sold in yards.
Necklines that carry embroidery

The neckline is the showpiece of a kaftan or boubou. Draft the neckline and the embroidery area together. Mark a clear rectangle or shield shape around the neck and down the front where the embroidery will go, and keep seams out of it. Interface the embroidery area with a stable woven or tear-away stabiliser so stitches do not pucker the fabric. If you send pieces to a machine embroiderer, send the cut panel with the neckline traced but **not cut**, plus a paper template of the design area, so the embroidery is placed exactly. Cut the neckline after embroidery, then face it.

For a men's grand boubou set, the robe is only one of three garments: the inner caftan and the trousers are drafted separately from their own measurements. Draft the inner caftan first, because the boubou must slip over it comfortably, and check the boubou neckline against the caftan collar so the two sit well together.
Respect the style's origin

Boubou and kaftan styles differ by region and community, and some details have meaning. When a client asks for a specific traditional style, ask her to show you an example and confirm the details rather than guessing.

A bespoke pattern is used once or twice. A **production pattern** is used dozens or hundreds of times, often by someone other than you. It must be complete, durable and impossible to misread. This lesson shows how to move from one good toile to a pattern set that can cut thirty aso-ebi gowns or a boutique order without mistakes.
What a production pattern set includes
**Every piece**, including facings, interfacing, linings, pockets, gussets and waistbands, each as its own piece. Nothing is "cut by eye".
**Seam allowances included** and stated, often a consistent width such as 1 cm or 1.5 cm on most seams so sewers do not have to think.
**Notches, drill holes and grain lines** on every piece, as in Module 1.
**A pattern plan or header card** listing all pieces, cut quantities, fabric, trims and the date of the last revision.
**Card, not paper**, for any pattern you will use more than a few times. Hang the full set on one hook.
A small production line
Production patterns let several people cut and sew the same style with the same result.
Markers and marker efficiency

A **marker** is the layout plan of all pattern pieces on the fabric, drawn on paper the width of the fabric. You arrange the pieces to use as little fabric as possible while keeping every grain line correct. Big pieces go down first, small pieces fill the gaps. When you find a good layout, trace it onto marker paper so you can reuse it.

**Marker efficiency** tells you how much of the fabric becomes garment and how much becomes waste. Efficiency percent = total area of pattern pieces divided by marker area (length times width), times 100. You can estimate pattern area by measuring each piece roughly as rectangles and triangles. Higher efficiency means lower fabric cost per garment.
Worked example: two markers for the same skirt
For example, Rukayat in Ilorin cuts flared skirts for a church choir order. Her pattern pieces total about 1.5 square metres per skirt. Fabric width is 1.5 m.
Marker A, one skirt at a time: marker length 1.4 m. Area = 1.4 times 1.5 = 2.1 square metres. Efficiency = 1.5 divided by 2.1 times 100, about 71 percent.

Marker B, two skirts nested together, with one set of pieces turned to fit into the curves of the other: length 2.4 m. Area = 2.4 times 1.5 = 3.6 square metres. Pattern area = 3.0. Efficiency = 3.0 divided by 3.6 times 100, about 83 percent.
Fabric per skirt: Marker A uses 1.4 m, Marker B uses 1.2 m.
For 20 skirts, Marker B saves 20 times 0.2 = 4 m of fabric.
She checks that turning pieces is allowed: the fabric is a plain solid with no nap, so it is.
By nesting two sizes or two copies in one marker, Rukayat saves 4 m on the order. For a one-way print or velvet she would not turn pieces, and would accept a lower efficiency.

Lays and multi-layer cutting

A **lay** is several layers of fabric spread on top of each other so you can cut many garments at once. Spread each layer flat and smooth, with selvedges lined up on one side and grain straight. Do not stretch the fabric as you spread. Place the marker on top, weight it or pin through all layers outside the pieces, and cut with long sharp shears or a rotary cutter, keeping the blade upright. Too many layers make lower pieces bigger than upper ones because the blade drifts, so start with a small number of layers and check pieces from the top and bottom of the lay against the pattern.
Cutting tools

Rotary cutters and electric cloth cutters are very sharp. Always close or guard the blade when you put it down, cut away from your body, and keep the other hand flat and well away from the cutting line. Never leave blades where children can reach them.

For lace and other fabrics where motif placement matters, multi-layer cutting is often not possible. Cut these in a single layer, piece by piece, and accept the extra time in your price. Mixed orders, such as aso-ebi where each guest brings her own fabric, also need single cutting, but you can still use the same production pattern set and the same cutting ticket system.
Cutting tickets

For every order, write a **cutting ticket**: style, sizes and quantities, fabric and colour, number of layers, marker used, date and who cut it. After cutting, count the pieces against the ticket before bundling. The ticket follows the bundle through sewing and inspection, so you always know where each garment is.

**Grading** is making a pattern bigger or smaller to fit a range of sizes while keeping the same style and proportions. In professional grading, you do not simply enlarge the whole pattern like a photocopy. You move specific points by planned amounts, because bodies do not grow evenly: a size larger is wider at the bust and hip, but the neck and shoulder grow only a little.
Shapes being resized
Grading resizes a pattern by moving key points, not by enlarging everything equally.
Key terms
**Base size**: the size you drafted and fitted, usually the middle of your range.
**Grade points** (also called cardinal points): corners and key positions on the pattern that move, such as neck point, shoulder point, underarm, waist at side seam and hem at side seam.
**Grade rule**: how far each grade point moves, written as a horizontal movement (x) and a vertical movement (y) between neighbouring sizes.
**Nest**: all graded sizes drawn on top of each other from the same reference point. A good nest shows evenly spaced, parallel lines.
From size chart to grade rules

Start from the size chart you built in Module 2. If your bust interval is 5 cm, each quarter pattern (front or back half of one side) must grow by 5 divided by 4 = 1.25 cm in width at bust level. That width is shared among points: some at the side seam, some at the shoulder and neck. Lengths also grow, but by smaller amounts, and you decide them from your length data.

Grading the sleeve to match

When the bodice armhole grows, the sleeve cap must grow to match, or the sleeve will not fit. Measure the graded armhole in each size and grade the sleeve so its cap length grows by the same amount, keeping the same cap ease you chose in Module 3. Grow the bicep width in step with your upper arm data. Sew-test the sleeve in the largest size, where problems show most.

She chooses a length grade of 1 cm per size, so XL is 2 cm longer than M at the hem.
Because the buba is kimono-cut, she moves the sleeve end outward by her sleeve length grade of 0.5 cm per size and keeps the underarm curve shape parallel.
She nests M, L and XL and checks that the lines are evenly spaced.
She sews the XL in calico on a willing XL client before cutting the production order.
The three sizes have the same style and proportions, and the XL test confirms the grade. She can now cut a mixed size order from one marker.

A **toile** (also called a muslin) is a test garment sewn from cheap fabric such as calico, close in weight to the final fabric. For complex bodies and expensive fabrics, the toile is where the real fitting happens. A good fitting is calm, structured and quick, and it gives you clear marks to take back to the pattern.
Preparing the toile
Cut from the pattern with all markings: centre front, centre back, bust points, waist line, hip line and grain lines drawn on the calico with a marker.
Sew with a long machine stitch so seams are easy to open, and sew seam allowances to the outside on one side if you want to pin changes easily.
Include one sleeve and the collar if the final garment has them.
Choose a calico of similar weight to the final fabric: a light calico for chiffon gowns, a heavier one for aso-oke or brocade.
A person fitting a piece into place
A toile is where each piece of the fit puzzle is checked before the real fabric is cut.
Fitting in a fixed order

Work from the top down, because changes at the shoulder affect everything below. Check the shoulders and neck first, then the bust, armhole and back, then the waist, then hips and hem, and finally the sleeve and collar. Fix the biggest problem first: a shoulder that is too wide can cause folds lower down that disappear once the shoulder is corrected.

Reading drag lines

**Drag lines** are diagonal or horizontal wrinkles caused by fabric pulling or collecting. The key rule: **drag lines point towards the problem**. Tight areas create pulling lines that radiate from the tight spot. Loose areas create soft folds that hang. Look at where the lines start and where they point.
Likely cause
Typical fix
Diagonal pulls from the bust towards the side seam and armhole
Not enough room over the bust
Full bust adjustment
Back too long for a sway back

Ask her to move
Before you finish, ask the client to sit, raise her arms, reach forward and walk a few steps. Many fit problems only appear in movement, and owambe gowns must survive dancing.

Keep the fitting professional and private. Fit in a screened corner or a separate room, with a mirror the client can see. Explain what you are checking as you go, ask before touching near the bust or hips, and keep pins pointing away from her skin. If the client is uncomfortable with you pinning close to the body, ask her to hold a section while you mark it, or have a female assistant present. Clients who feel safe and respected at fittings become your most loyal clients.
Marking and recording

Pin changes symmetrically unless the body is asymmetric. Mark new seam lines on the calico with a marker in a different colour, and write the amount beside each change, for example "take in 1 cm" or "add 2 cm". Take photos from front, side and back with consent. Before the client leaves, transfer each change to her order card. Do not trust memory after a busy day.

With shoulders fixed, the bust pulls are still there. She unpicks the side seam at bust level and the toile springs open by about 2 cm on each side: she notes "FBA about 2 cm each side".
At the back she pinches out a horizontal fold of about 1.5 cm at the centre back waist, tapering to nothing at the side seam.
She asks the client to sit and raise her arms. Everything holds.
She writes all three changes on the toile and the order card and photographs the marked toile.
Grace leaves the fitting with three clear pattern changes, each with an amount. Fixing in order stopped her from chasing folds that were really caused by the shoulder.

Pattern alterations for complex bodies: full bust, sway back, shoulders and arms
Perform a full bust adjustment on a darted bodice and on a princess pattern
Correct a sway back on the pattern

Widen a sleeve for a fuller upper arm

The toile tells you what is wrong. The pattern is where you fix it permanently. This lesson covers the four alterations you will make most often for real clients. Each one adds or removes length or width only where the body needs it, so the rest of the pattern stays balanced. Always alter a copy and keep the original.
Full bust adjustment (FBA) on a darted bodice

Mark the bust point. Draw line 1 from the bust point straight down to the waist, parallel to the grain. Draw line 2 from the bust point up to about one third of the way up the armhole. Draw line 3 through the middle of the side dart to the bust point.
Cut line 1 up to the bust point and continue along line 2 to the armhole edge, leaving a tiny hinge at the armhole. Cut line 3 to the bust point, leaving a hinge there too.
Spread the side section outward at bust level by the amount needed for half the extra bust room. If the total extra needed is 4 cm, spread 2 cm on each half pattern.
The side dart opens wider and the front becomes longer at the side. Cut horizontally across the centre front section at waist level and drop it to match the new length.
Redraw the darts to the bust point (shortened slightly so they end before it), true the side seam and waist, and check the armhole has kept its shape.
A pushpin
Each alteration pivots on a fixed point, such as the bust point, so the rest of the pattern stays balanced.
Choosing an alteration
Add width: full bust, broad back
Add length: rounded back, full tummy
Remove width: narrow shoulders
Remove length: sway back
Width change
Length change
Name whether the body needs more or less width or length, then choose the matching alteration.
FBA on a princess pattern

On a princess pattern, the bust shaping lives in the side front panel. Add width to the side front panel at bust level, spreading the curve outward over the bust and blending back to the original line at the armhole and waist. Add a matching amount of length over the bust curve so it does not pull up, then add the same length to the centre front panel between the bust notches, or ease it in. Re-true the seam and move the bust notches.

On the back bodice, draw a horizontal line a few centimetres above the waist, from centre back to the side seam. Fold out a wedge that is widest at centre back (the amount you pinched at the fitting, for example 1.5 cm) and tapers to nothing at the side seam. Redraw the centre back as a straight line; if the centre back is on a fold, the grain line may need to shift so the fold edge stays straight. For a gown, make the same change on the back skirt at the waist.
Sloping and square shoulders

For **sloping shoulders**, lower the shoulder point by the amount found at the fitting and redraw the shoulder line from the neck point. Then lower the underarm point on the side seam by the same amount, so the armhole keeps its size and the sleeve still fits. For **square shoulders**, raise both by the same amount. If only one shoulder slopes, make the change on that side only and cut the front and back as full, unfolded pieces, or use a slightly thicker shoulder pad on the low side.
Fuller upper arm

On the sleeve, draw a line down the centre from the crown to the hem, and a line across at the bicep. Cut the centre line from hem to just below the crown, then cut along the bicep line from the centre almost to each underarm point. Spread the centre line by the extra width needed; the cap drops slightly as it opens. Redraw the cap, check the new cap length against the armhole and adjust the cap ease. If the sleeve cap becomes too long, you may need to lower the underarm on the bodice slightly.
Worked example: altering a client's pattern after fitting

For example, Grace from the previous lesson has three recorded changes for her client's lace sheath gown: lower the shoulder 1 cm, FBA 2 cm each side, sway back 1.5 cm. The client also has a bicep of 36 cm and the sleeve measures 34 cm at the bicep.
Shoulder: she lowers the front and back shoulder points by 1 cm and lowers the underarm by 1 cm, keeping the armhole length unchanged.
FBA: she spreads the side front panel 2 cm at bust level, blending to the armhole and waist, adds matching length over the bust and re-trues with the centre front panel.
Sway back: she folds out a 1.5 cm wedge on the back bodice and back skirt at centre back, tapering to the side.
Sleeve: she wants 3 cm of ease over the 36 cm bicep, so the sleeve needs 39 cm, which is 5 cm more than the current 34 cm. She spreads the sleeve centre by 5 cm and redraws the cap.
She measures the armhole and new sleeve cap and finds 5 cm of cap ease, more than she wants. She flattens the cap until the ease is 3 cm.
She sews a second, quick toile of the bodice and sleeve to confirm.
The second toile fits with no drag lines, and the client can lift her arms freely. Grace saves the altered pattern under the client's name with all amounts recorded for future orders.
Do not skip the second toile
When you make three or more changes, a second quick toile is cheaper than recutting lace. Changes interact: a lower shoulder and a wider sleeve both affect the armhole.

Quality control (QC) is not one look at the end. It is a system of checks at every stage so problems are caught when they are cheap to fix. A crooked dart found before the side seams are sewn takes two minutes to correct. The same dart found after the lining and zip are in can take an hour, or may not be fixable at all on lace.
Three layers of quality control
Layers of quality control
Final inspection
In-process checks
Correct patterns and cutting
Most quality is built at the bottom; the final inspection only confirms it.
**Correct patterns and cutting**: tested patterns, correct grain, notches cut, pieces counted against the cutting ticket.
**In-process checks**: at set points, for example after darts and before closing seams, after attaching the bodice to the skirt, after the zip.
**Final inspection**: measurements, appearance, finishing, pressing and packing.
Tolerances

A **tolerance** is how far a finished measurement may differ from the specification. For example, you might allow plus or minus 0.5 cm on a collar length or a bust measurement, and plus or minus 1 cm on a gown length. Tight tolerances are needed where small errors show, such as collars, cuffs and matched seams. Choose your own numbers, write them on a specification sheet for each style and measure against them, not against "looks fine".

What to check
Example tolerance
After darts
Same length, same position left and right, pressed correctly
Within 0.3 cm left to right
After side seams
Bust, waist, hip measured flat against the spec
Within 0.5 cm of spec
After zip
Waist seams match across the zip, zip flat, no ripples
Seams meet exactly
Final
Length, sleeve length, hem level, collar symmetry
Length within 1 cm, collar points within 0.3 cm
A person inspecting work closely
Inspection against written tolerances turns "looks fine" into a measurable standard.
Final inspection routine
Inspect on a dress form or hanger in good daylight or bright white light.
Outside: seams straight, prints and stripes matched, hem level, no puckers, no shine from pressing, no chalk or marker visible.
Inside: threads trimmed, seams finished, lining sitting well, no raw edges in unlined areas.
Function: zip runs smoothly, buttons secure and aligned with buttonholes, hooks fastened.
Measurements: check key measurements against the spec sheet and tolerances.
Final press, hang, cover and attach the care card.
Inspecting a batch

For a production order, inspect every piece if the order is small or high value, such as twenty aso-ebi gowns for one wedding. For larger repeat orders, some businesses inspect a sample from each batch and inspect everything if the sample shows problems. Large factories use formal sampling plans, but for a small workroom the safer rule is: if in doubt, inspect all. Always inspect the first garment off the line fully before sewing the rest, because a mistake in the first piece will be repeated in every piece.

Do not forget the finishing details clients notice first. Hand-sewn beads must be secured with knots every few beads, so one broken thread does not release a whole line. Hooks and eyes on a gown should sit exactly at the waist seam. Lining hems should sit about 2 to 3 cm above the outer hem so they never peep out. Labels, if you use them, should be stitched straight and flat, not scratching the neck. These small points are what separate a premium garment from an ordinary one.

For example, Ronke in Ibadan and two apprentices are sewing 24 identical aso-ebi gowns for a wedding in three weeks.
She fully inspects the first finished gown and finds the waist seam does not match at the zip by 0.5 cm. She corrects the sewing method before the others are sewn.
She sets checkpoints after darts, after side seams and after the zip, and adds a tick box to each bundle ticket.
At final inspection she logs defects: 3 loose threads, 2 uneven hems, 1 crooked zip.
The crooked zip and the hems are fixed. She notes that both hems came from one apprentice and shows her how to mark the hem from the floor.
Total: 24 gowns delivered on time, all passing final inspection.
Catching the zip issue on the first gown saved fixing 24. The defect log shows where training is needed, which improves the next order.

Take a front, back and inside photo of every finished garment before handover. It protects you in any dispute and builds your portfolio, with the client's permission to share.
