At advanced level, your skills are worth more, and your clients expect more: clear communication, reliable dates and garments that match what was agreed. Professional client work protects both you and the client. It turns "I thought you said" arguments into a simple check of what was written.
The design consultation
**Event and date**: what the garment is for, and the date it must be ready. Agree a delivery date at least a few days before the event.
**Style reference**: ask for photos and discuss what she likes in each one. Sketch the agreed design, front and back, on paper or in a phone app, and send her a photo.
**Fabric**: who supplies it, how much, whether it has been tested for shrinkage, lining choice.
**Fittings**: how many, and roughly when. Complex gowns usually need a toile fitting and at least one fitting in the real fabric.
**Price, deposit and balance**: written down, with what happens if dates or design change.
A person reviewing a contract document
A short written order form protects both tailor and client.
The written order form

One page is enough: client name and phone, order number, design sketch or photo, fabric details, measurements reference, fitting dates, delivery date, total price, deposit paid, balance due, and your terms. Common terms include: the deposit is not refundable once fabric is cut; design changes after cutting may cost extra; late arrival for fittings may move the delivery date. Send it on WhatsApp and ask the client to reply "agreed". That message is your record.
Pricing from measured time

Advanced pieces vary too much for a fixed price list. Price from **time, materials and overheads**. Time yourself on each stage of a few garments: drafting, toile, fitting, cutting, sewing, finishing. Decide an hourly rate for your skill level. Add materials you supply (lining, interfacing, zip, thread, beads), and a share of overheads such as power, fuel, rent and machine repairs. Then add your profit margin.

Profit
Overheads share

Worked example: pricing a corset lace gown
For example, Nkechi in Lagos is pricing a corset lace gown with a full toile fitting. All naira amounts are approximate examples only, not market prices.
From her time records: consultation and drafting 3 hours, toile and fitting 4 hours, cutting lace 3 hours, sewing and boning 12 hours, beading and finishing 6 hours. Total 28 hours.
She sets her hourly rate at 2,500 naira for this level of work: 28 times 2,500 = 70,000 naira.
Materials she supplies: lining, boning, zip, interfacing, thread, extra beads, about 25,000 naira.
Overheads share for 28 hours, including generator fuel: about 8,000 naira.
Subtotal 103,000 naira. She adds 20 percent profit: 103,000 times 1.2 = 123,600 naira, and quotes 125,000 naira.
She asks for a 60 percent deposit (75,000 naira) before cutting, with the balance at final fitting.
Nkechi can explain her price line by line. If a client pushes back, she can offer a simpler design with fewer hours instead of cutting her rate.

Track your real hourly earnings over time. If many quotes are refused, look at where your hours go before lowering your rate: a faster drafting method, a production pattern for a style you sell often, or batching similar tasks may cut hours without cutting quality. If almost every quote is accepted at once, your rate may be lower than your market will pay, so raise it gradually and watch the response.
Safe payments
Payment scams

Confirm every transfer in your own bank or wallet app (for example Moniepoint, Opay or your bank app) before releasing a garment. Never rely on a screenshot or an SMS alert alone, as both can be faked. Do not share OTPs or PINs with anyone claiming to be from your bank.

Group orders bring volume but can become chaotic. Appoint one coordinator on the client side. Set a firm last date for measurements and fabric collection, a few weeks before the event. Keep a spreadsheet with each person's name, phone, measurements date, fabric received, deposit, fitting date, balance and collection. Use your production patterns and graded sizes where styles are identical, and the QC checklist from the previous lesson for every piece. Say no politely to late additions you cannot finish well: one rushed garment can damage the reputation you have built on the rest.

Write the cut quantity, for example, cut 2 self, cut 2 lining, or cut 1 on fold.
Draw the grain line the full length of the piece, with arrow heads at both ends, so the cutter can measure from the selvedge at two points.
Use one notch on the front armhole and two on the back, so a front sleeve can never go into a back armhole. Punch dart drill holes about 1 cm inside the true point.
And state the seam allowance. If anything is missing, the cutter has to guess, and guesses cost fabric.
Fabric behaviour
Straight grain or true bias?
Used for most pieces
Binding and cowls
The lengthwise grain runs parallel to the selvedge, the finished edge. It is the strongest direction and stretches least, so most pieces are cut on it.
The true bias is the diagonal at 45 degrees. To find it, fold the crosswise edge along the selvedge. Bias stretches and drapes.
Hang a bias-cut skirt for at least a day before you level the hem, because the bias drops unevenly.
Test before you cut
The shrinkage test
Shrinkage percent = (before minus after) ÷ before × 100
Cut a 50 cm by 50 cm square on the grain
Mark the lengthwise direction
Wash and dry it as the client will, then press
Measure both directions again
Work out the percent and record it
Cotton, linen and many ankara prints shrink when first washed. A fitted gown cut to exact size can become too tight. So test first. Cut a square of 50 cm by 50 cm along the grain.
Wash and dry it the way the client will, for example hand wash and line dry. Then press it.
For example, Bisi in Ibadan tested a cotton print. The lengthwise side now measured 48.5 cm, and the crosswise side 49.5 cm.
50 minus 48.5, divided by 50, times 100, is 3 percent lengthwise. Crosswise it is 1 percent. A 110 cm dress would lose about 3.3 cm after the first wash.
So Bisi washed, dried and pressed the whole fabric before cutting, and wrote it on the order card.
Workroom flow
Work moves forward, never back
Receive: tag fabric with name and due date
Cut on a clear table, then bundle
Sew, with good light at each machine
Press close to the machines
Finish, inspect and pack
When orders grow, the problem is rarely sewing skill. It is flow. Tag every client's fabric with her name, order number and due date the moment it arrives.
Cut on the largest clear table, then tie all pieces of one garment together with its tag, zip, buttons and lining, so the sewer never searches.
Put a bright white LED lamp at each machine, and keep pressing close by, because you press after almost every seam.
Then finish, inspect and pack. For example, Hauwa in Kaduna timed herself and added an overlocker first, because it removed her slowest step.

Never plug several machines and an iron into one board. Irons draw a lot of current and boards can overheat.
Run generators outside, never in a closed room. The exhaust has carbon monoxide, which can kill without warning.
Unplug the iron when not in use. Switch off a machine before changing a needle or clearing a jam.

Why it matters
Same numbers, different bodies
Basic numbers hide shape
Shape measurements show where width is
Posture decides where wrinkles appear
Checks catch errors before cutting
Two women with a 100 cm bust can need completely different patterns. Shape measurements reveal where each body carries its width.
Posture matters too. One client leans back, another rounds her shoulders. These decide where wrinkles will appear.
And one wrong number can ruin a gown, so we build checks into the routine.
Worked example
Ngozi reads the bust numbers
Large difference: draft the frame from high bust, then add bust.
High bust 92 cm, full bust 104 cm
Difference: 104 minus 92 = 12 cm
Frame is closer to a 92 cm body
Bust span 20 cm: 10 cm each side
Bust depth 27 cm sets dart height
Take the high bust high under the arms, and the full bust over the fullest part. Ask her to wear the bra she will wear with the garment.
For example, Ngozi in Port Harcourt measures a client: high bust 92 cm, full bust 104 cm.
The difference is 12 cm. That is large.
So her shoulders and back are closer to a 92 cm body. Drafting from 104 would make the neckline too wide and the armhole gape.
The bust span of 20 cm means each bust point sits 10 cm from centre front.
And the bust depth of 27 cm sets how low the bust point sits, so darts and princess seams aim at the right place.
Ngozi drafts the frame from the smaller number and adds bust width with a bust adjustment. Her first toile sits correctly.
Reading the figure
Posture predicts pattern changes
Sway back: shorten back waist length
Rounded upper back: more back length
Full tummy: extra front length and width
Prominent seat: deeper back darts, length
Uneven shoulders: adjust one side
Ask her to stand naturally, and look from the front, side and back.
A deep hollow at the lower back is a sway back. It gives folds above the back waist, so shorten the back waist length.
A rounded upper back makes the back pull up, so it needs more back length and width.
A full tummy makes the front hem rise. The front needs extra length and width.
A prominent seat makes the back skirt ride up, so deepen the back darts and add length.
Use neutral words. Say, your back has a lovely curve, so I will shorten the back waist. Never make her feel judged.

Front, side and back photos help you compare fittings. Take them only with clear permission, in fitted everyday clothing, keep them locked, and delete them when the order is complete.
Never take them undressed, and never post them or send them to anyone. Nigeria's Data Protection Act 2023 sets duties for anyone handling personal data.
Size charts
Build a chart from your own clients
Copy bust, waist, hip from client cards
Sort by bust; find the biggest cluster
Base size where most clients are
Choose an interval from your data
Publish body and finished garment charts
Imported size charts often do not match your clients, especially at the hip. Build your own from your cards, using numbers instead of names.
For example, Tola in Lagos has 60 past client cards. Most fall between 92 and 112 cm bust, with the biggest cluster around 100 to 104 cm.
She makes that her base size, M, because fitting errors are smallest near the middle.
With a 5 cm interval she gets S, M, L and XL, and sets hip ranges from her own data.
She adds 16 cm of ease for the buba and publishes both the body chart and the finished garment chart, with centimetre ranges beside every size name.
Chioma catches a wrong number
Measured: bust 98 cm, hip 104 cm
Her favourite dress: 100 cm at hip
A woven dress cannot be smaller
Re-measured hip: 98 cm
A 6 cm error caught before cutting
Cross-checks catch errors. Take bust, waist and hip twice. If readings differ by more than about 1 cm, take a third. Then measure a garment she loves.
For example, Chioma in Abuja measures a bust of 98 cm and a hip of 104 cm.
The client's well-fitting dress measures 50 cm flat at the hip. Doubled, that is 100 cm around.
That is smaller than her measured hip, which is impossible for a woven dress without stretch. So one number is wrong.
Chioma re-measures with the client's feet together and gets 98 cm. The tape had dipped at the back.
She corrects the card, writes the date, and never overwrites old numbers. A 6 cm error was caught, and the client never knew.

The big idea
Change a tested block on paper
The block already fits
Every new style keeps that fit
Always work on a copy
Flat-pattern manipulation means changing a tested block on paper to make a new style. Because the block already fits, every new style keeps that fit at the neck, shoulder, bust and waist.
Always work on a copy, never the master, with grain line, bust point and notches marked.
After every change, true the new seams: check that edges sewn together are the same length. Fix it on paper, never on fabric.
Two methods
Slash and spread, or pivot
Cut lines on a copy
Trace, then rotate the block
Turn around a fixed point
Fast once practised
No cutting of the master
With slash and spread, you cut lines on a copy and open them to add width. For a flared skirt, slash from the dart point to the hem and close the dart. The dart becomes flare at the hem.
With pivot, you hold the paper down with an awl on the bust point and rotate the block to close a dart. Both give the same result.
Worked example
Zainab's gathered peplum
Soft gathers: about 1.5 times. Heavy gathers: about 2 times.
Front waist on the quarter: 20 cm
Wanted fullness: 1.5 times = 30 cm
Draw a 20 cm by 15 cm rectangle
Slash into 5 strips, spread 2.5 cm each
Notch, then test in calico
For example, Zainab in Abuja makes a yoked blouse with a gathered peplum for an ankara set. Her front waist on the quarter pattern is 20 cm.
She wants 1.5 times fullness, so the top edge of the peplum needs 30 cm.
She draws a rectangle 20 cm by 15 cm.
She slashes it into five strips and spreads each gap by 2.5 cm at the top, giving 30 cm.
She marks notches and tests the peplum in calico before cutting the ankara.
Chiffon gathers beautifully at 2 times, but a stiff aso-oke would look bulky. Test on a strip of your own fabric first.
Princess lines
Share the change across panels
Waist 6 cm too big, bust and hip fine
6 seams, so 12 edges
6 cm ÷ 12 = 0.5 cm per edge
Blend back about 10 cm above and below
Re-true seams; change lining too

A princess seam is a full seam over the bust, so each panel can be shaped on its own. For example, Efe in Benin City makes a lace mermaid gown. At the toile fitting the waist is 6 cm too big all round.
The gown has front and back princess seams plus two side seams. That is six seams, and twelve edges.
So she takes 0.5 cm from each edge at the waist, not all from the side seams.
She blends back to the original line about 10 cm above and below.
Then she re-trues every seam pair and changes the lining too. The grain stays straight and the lace stays balanced.
Sleeves
Draft the sleeve from the armhole
Sew one calico test sleeve before cutting lace.
Armhole: 22 + 23.5 = 45.5 cm
Add about 3 cm cap ease: about 48.5 cm
Bicep too narrow? Lower the cap 1 cm
Cap curve 49.5 cm? Flatten near crown
Final cap: 48.6 cm, then test
The sleeve cap must match the armhole, plus a small planned extra called cap ease. For example, Adaeze in Owerri measures a front armhole of 22 cm and a back of 23.5 cm. Total, 45.5 cm.
For crepe she wants about 3 cm of cap ease, so the cap curve should be about 48.5 cm.
Her first draft gave a bicep of 31 cm, less than the client's 32 cm arm. A lower cap makes a wider sleeve, so she lowers it by 1 cm. The bicep becomes about 34 cm.
The new cap curve measures 49.5 cm, too long. She flattens it slightly near the crown.
Now it is 48.6 cm. Remember, a high cap looks elegant but limits arm lift. A low cap gives more movement.
Sleeves are cheap to test and expensive to get wrong in lace. Sew a calico sleeve into the toile and check it hangs without twisting.
Collars
Three collars from the neckline
Rectangle, half neckline long. Raise the front end 1 to 1.5 cm so it hugs the neck.
Overlap shoulders 1 to 2 cm at the armhole end. This gives a slight roll that hides the seam.
Stand curves upward; collar curves downward at front. Collar 1 to 1.5 cm deeper at back.

Every collar starts from the neckline length measured on the pattern. For a mandarin stand, draw a rectangle half the neckline long. Raise the front end of the lower edge by 1 to 1.5 cm, so it hugs the neck.
For a Peter Pan collar, overlap the shoulders by 1 to 2 cm at the armhole end. That gives a slight roll that hides the seam.
For a shirt collar, the stand curves upward but the collar curves downward at the front, and the collar is 1 to 1.5 cm deeper at the back.
Staystitch the neckline right after cutting, so it does not stretch.

Share fit changes across all panel seams
Collars start from the measured neckline

Worked example
Yetunde drafts a buba and iro
Test in calico: lift both arms and dance a few steps.
Bust 104 + 20 ease, ÷ 4 = 31 cm a quarter
Hip check: (112 + 8) ÷ 4 = 30 cm, so fine
Closer sleeve: 10 cm bias gusset
Iro: 4 cm waistband, 25 cm front overlap
Hooks and bars so it stays for dancing

A kimono-cut buba is a T-shape, with the sleeve cut in one with the body. For example, Yetunde in Abeokuta drafts for a client with a 104 cm bust. She chooses 20 cm of ease, so each quarter is 31 cm at bust level.
She checks the hip: 112 plus 8, divided by 4, needs 30 cm. Her 31 cm side line is enough, so the side seam runs straight.
The client wants a closer sleeve, which can pull up and tear at the underarm. So Yetunde adds a bias-cut gusset of 10 cm by 10 cm at each underarm.

Calculate before you buy
Hadiza plans a boubou
Arm span 158 cm, fabric 116 cm wide
Shortfall 42 cm: two side panels
Length: 2 × 138 + hems = 282 cm
Total: 564 cm, about 5.64 m
6 yards is short, so buy 7 yards

A boubou is built from rectangles folded at the shoulder, spanning wrist to wrist. Check fabric width first. For example, Hadiza in Kano has a client with an arm span of 158 cm, but her fabric is only 116 cm wide.
The shortfall is 42 cm, so she adds two symmetrical side panels, each 24 cm wide with seam allowance.
The centre panel is 2 times 138, plus 3 cm hem at each end. That is 282 cm. The side panels fit side by side in one more length.
So she needs 564 cm, about 5.64 m, plus some for facing and print matching.
6 yards is only about 5.49 m, which is not enough, so she buys 7. One yard is 0.9144 m, so always convert carefully.

Marker A, one skirt: 1.4 m long
2.1 square metres, about 71 percent
Marker B, two nested: 2.4 m long
3.6 square metres, about 83 percent
20 skirts: saves 4 m of fabric
A boubou is built from rectangles folded at the shoulder. Check fabric width first. For example, Hadiza in Kano has a client with a 158 cm arm span, but her fabric is 116 cm wide.
Marker A, one skirt at a time, is 1.4 m long. That is 2.1 square metres, so the efficiency is about 71 percent.
The centre panel is 2 times 138, plus 3 cm hem at each end: 282 cm. The side panels need one more length.
That is 3.6 square metres for 3.0 of pattern, about 83 percent.
Each skirt now uses 1.2 m instead of 1.4, so 20 skirts save 4 m. But only turn pieces on plain fabric with no nap. Never on a one-way print or velvet.

Cutting blades and lays
Close or guard rotary and electric cutters every time you put them down.
Cut away from your body. Keep your other hand flat and well away from the cutting line.
Never leave blades where children can reach them.
A marker is the layout of all pieces on the fabric. For example, Rukayat in Ilorin cuts choir skirts. Each skirt's pieces total about 1.5 square metres, on 1.5 m wide fabric.

The paid-for level
What clients pay most for
A calm, structured toile fitting
Fixes made on the pattern
Checks at every stage
Clear orders and fair prices

This module brings everything together at the level clients pay most for. A toile is a test garment sewn from calico of similar weight to the final fabric. The real fitting happens there, and the fixes go onto the pattern.
Then you will build quality checks into every stage, and run client work with written orders and prices you can explain.
Drag lines
Drag lines point to the problem
Fit from the top down
Bust to side seam pulls: full bust
Folds above back waist: sway back
Neck to armhole folds: sloping shoulders
Ask her to sit, reach and walk

Fit from the top down, because a change at the shoulder affects everything below. Fix the biggest problem first. Drag lines are wrinkles from fabric pulling or collecting, and they point towards the problem.
Diagonal pulls from the bust towards the side seam mean not enough room over the bust.
Horizontal folds just above the back waist mean the back is too long for a sway back.
Diagonal folds from the neck towards the armhole mean her shoulders slope more than the pattern.
Before you finish, ask her to sit, raise her arms, reach forward and walk. Owambe gowns must survive dancing. Fit in a private, screened corner, and ask before touching near the bust or hips.
Worked example
Grace fits and alters a lace gown
Three or more changes? Sew a second quick toile.
Shoulder 1 cm lower; underarm 1 cm lower
Full bust: spread side panel 2 cm
Sway back: fold out a 1.5 cm wedge
Sleeve: 36 cm bicep + 3 cm ease = 39 cm
Recheck cap ease; flatten to 3 cm

For example, Grace in Calabar fits a toile for a lace sheath gown. She starts at the top. Re-pinning the shoulder 1 cm lower removes the neck-to-armhole folds. On the pattern she lowers the underarm by 1 cm too, so the armhole keeps its size.
The bust pulls remain. Unpicked at the side seam, the toile springs open about 2 cm each side. So she spreads the side front panel 2 cm at bust level and adds matching length.
At the back she pinches out about 1.5 cm at centre back waist, tapering to nothing at the side seam, and folds out that wedge on the pattern.
The client's bicep is 36 cm, and the sleeve is only 34. With 3 cm of ease she needs 39, so she spreads the sleeve 5 cm.
The new cap now has 5 cm of ease, too much, so she flattens it to 3 cm.
Changes interact, so she sews a second quick toile. It is cheaper than recutting lace, and it fits with no drag lines.
Quality control
Check at every stage
After darts: within 0.3 cm left to right
After side seams: within 0.5 cm of spec
After zip: waist seams meet exactly
Final: length within 1 cm
First garment of a batch fully inspected
Photograph front, back and inside
A crooked dart found early takes two minutes to fix. Found after the lining and zip, it can take an hour. So check at set points against tolerances written on a spec sheet, not against looks fine.
For example, Ronke in Ibadan sewed 24 aso-ebi gowns. She fully inspected the first gown and found the waist seam missed at the zip by 0.5 cm. Fixing the method then saved fixing 24.
Photograph every finished garment before handover. It protects you in any dispute.

Nkechi prices a corset lace gown

Materials she supplies
Overheads, including fuel
